description: Synthetic but realistic PubMed-style abstracts for AegisHealth-KG vector retrieval. These mimic real research but are fabricated for the prototype. The system's vector search engine will index these and retrieve relevant abstracts when building appeal evidence.
note: All PMIDs, DOIs, authors, and journal names are fictional. These abstracts are designed to be realistic enough for the vector search to demonstrate meaningful retrieval but must NOT be cited as real research.

articles.title: Continuous Glucose Monitoring Improves Glycemic Control in Type 2 Diabetes Patients with Prior Oral Therapy Failure: A Randomized Controlled Trial
articles.journal: Journal of Diabetes Technology and Therapeutics
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) who fail first-line and second-line oral hypoglycemic therapies face limited treatment options. Continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) has shown promise in improving glycemic control, but evidence in this specific population is limited. METHODS: We conducted a multicenter randomized controlled trial of 312 adults with T2DM who had documented failure of both metformin and a sulfonylurea agent. Participants were randomized 1:1 to CGM (Dexcom G6) plus standard care versus standard care alone. Primary outcome was change in HbA1c at 6 months. Secondary outcomes included time in range (70-180 mg/dL), hypoglycemic events, and patient satisfaction. RESULTS: At 6 months, the CGM group demonstrated significantly greater HbA1c reduction compared to control (-1.4% vs -0.3%, p<0.001). Time in range increased by 18.2 percentage points in the CGM group versus 3.1 in controls (p<0.001). CGM users experienced 62% fewer hypoglycemic events (p=0.003). Patient satisfaction scores were significantly higher in the CGM group (DTSQ: 28.4 vs 19.2, p<0.001). CONCLUSION: CGM significantly improves glycemic control, reduces hypoglycemia, and improves satisfaction in T2DM patients who have failed oral therapy step protocols. These findings support CGM as a medically necessary intervention for patients with documented oral therapy failure.
articles.relevance: Directly supports Scenario 1 appeal — demonstrates CGM efficacy in patients who have failed metformin and sulfonylurea step therapy

articles.title: Real-World Outcomes of CGM Adoption Following Step Therapy Protocol Completion in a Large Commercial Insurance Population
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVE: To evaluate glycemic outcomes and healthcare utilization following CGM initiation in commercially insured patients with T2DM who completed step therapy protocols (documented failure of ≥2 oral agents). RESEARCH DESIGN AND METHODS: Retrospective cohort study of 1,847 patients from a large commercial claims database (2018-2021) who initiated CGM after completing step therapy requirements. Outcomes were compared to 3,694 propensity-matched controls who continued non-CGM management. RESULTS: CGM adoption was associated with a mean HbA1c reduction of 1.1% at 12 months (95% CI: -1.3 to -0.9, p<0.001). Emergency department visits for hypoglycemia decreased by 47% (IRR 0.53, 95% CI: 0.38-0.74). Total diabetes-related healthcare costs decreased by $2,340 per patient per year (p=0.01) despite the added cost of CGM supplies, driven primarily by reduced ED visits and inpatient admissions. Patients with baseline HbA1c >8.0% benefited most from CGM (HbA1c reduction: -1.6%). CONCLUSIONS: In patients who have failed step therapy protocols, CGM adoption is associated with clinically meaningful glycemic improvement, reduced hypoglycemic emergencies, and net cost savings. Step therapy failures represent a population with clear medical necessity for CGM.
articles.relevance: Supports Scenario 1 — real-world evidence that CGM is beneficial and cost-effective specifically in patients who have completed and failed step therapy

articles.title: Hypoglycemia Risk Stratification in Type 2 Diabetes: The Case for Continuous Glucose Monitoring in Sulfonylurea-Exposed Patients
articles.abstract: Sulfonylurea-induced hypoglycemia remains a significant clinical concern in the management of type 2 diabetes mellitus. This review examines the evidence base for continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) as a risk mitigation strategy in patients with a documented history of sulfonylurea-related hypoglycemic events. We analyzed 23 studies (N=4,512) and found that patients with ≥3 prior hypoglycemic events while on sulfonylurea therapy had a 3.8-fold increased risk of severe hypoglycemia (95% CI: 2.9-5.0) and a 2.1-fold increased risk of hypoglycemia-related emergency department visits (95% CI: 1.6-2.8). CGM utilization in this high-risk population was associated with a 58-71% reduction in hypoglycemic events across studies. We propose that patients meeting the following criteria have clear medical necessity for CGM: (1) documented trial and failure of metformin, (2) documented trial of sulfonylurea with ≥3 hypoglycemic events, and (3) persistent glycemic instability (HbA1c >7.5%). These findings challenge step therapy protocols that delay CGM access for patients who have already demonstrated oral therapy failure and hypoglycemia risk.
articles.relevance: Supports Scenario 1 — directly addresses hypoglycemia risk in sulfonylurea-exposed patients (the patient had 5 hypo events including ER visit)

articles.title: Optimal Duration of Conservative Physical Therapy Before MRI in Knee Pain: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Insurance payers commonly require a trial of conservative physical therapy before authorizing MRI for knee pain. However, the optimal duration of conservative therapy before imaging remains unclear. METHODS: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 18 studies (N=6,234 patients) examining the relationship between duration of physical therapy trial and diagnostic imaging outcomes in patients with non-traumatic knee pain. RESULTS: Patients who did not improve after 4-6 weeks of structured physical therapy (≥2 sessions/week) were significantly more likely to have structural pathology identified on MRI (OR 3.2, 95% CI: 2.4-4.3). There was no significant difference in MRI diagnostic yield between 4-week, 6-week, and 8-week PT trial durations (p=0.42), suggesting that a 4-week trial is diagnostically equivalent to longer protocols. Positive clinical examination findings (McMurray test, joint effusion, mechanical symptoms) increased MRI diagnostic yield regardless of PT duration (OR 5.1, 95% CI: 3.8-6.9). CONCLUSIONS: A 4-6 week trial of physical therapy is sufficient to identify patients who require advanced imaging. Strict 6-week minimums may unnecessarily delay diagnosis without improving diagnostic accuracy, particularly when clinical examination findings strongly suggest internal derangement.
articles.relevance: Supports Scenario 2 appeal — evidence that 4-6 week PT trial is sufficient and strict 6-week requirements may delay necessary diagnosis, especially with positive McMurray test

articles.title: Clinical Examination Accuracy for Medial Meniscal Tears: McMurray Test Sensitivity and the Role of Early MRI
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: The McMurray test remains a widely used clinical examination maneuver for detecting meniscal tears, but its diagnostic performance and implications for imaging authorization are debated. METHODS: Prospective diagnostic accuracy study of 482 patients presenting with knee pain and suspected meniscal pathology. All patients underwent standardized clinical examination including McMurray test, followed by MRI within 2 weeks. MRI findings served as the reference standard. RESULTS: The McMurray test demonstrated a sensitivity of 71% (95% CI: 65-77%) and specificity of 85% (95% CI: 80-90%) for medial meniscal tears. When combined with joint line tenderness, sensitivity increased to 89% (95% CI: 84-93%). A positive McMurray test with effusion had a positive predictive value of 92% for meniscal pathology. In patients with positive McMurray test, the mean delay from clinical examination to MRI due to prior authorization requirements was 23 days (SD 14 days), during which 34% of patients reported worsening symptoms. CONCLUSIONS: A positive McMurray test, particularly with joint effusion, is highly predictive of meniscal pathology and should be considered sufficient clinical indication for MRI authorization. Extended conservative therapy requirements in the presence of clear clinical signs may delay diagnosis and treatment without clinical benefit.
articles.relevance: Supports Scenario 2 — positive McMurray test with effusion has 92% PPV for meniscal pathology, supporting the clinical need for MRI

articles.title: Optimal Duration of Cognitive Behavioral Therapy for Recurrent Major Depressive Disorder: A Systematic Review of Dose-Response Relationships
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Arbitrary session limits on psychotherapy may not reflect evidence-based treatment durations, particularly for recurrent major depressive disorder (MDD). We examined the dose-response relationship for CBT in recurrent MDD to determine optimal treatment duration. METHODS: Systematic review of 31 randomized controlled trials (N=4,892) examining CBT for recurrent MDD (≥2 episodes). We analyzed the relationship between number of sessions and outcomes: remission (PHQ-9 <5), response (≥50% PHQ-9 reduction), and relapse rates at 12-month follow-up. RESULTS: The probability of achieving remission increased significantly with session count: 22% at 12 sessions, 38% at 16 sessions, 52% at 20 sessions, and 64% at 24 sessions (dose-response curve, p<0.001 for trend). For patients with recurrent MDD who achieved PHQ-9 scores in the moderate range (10-14) by session 20, extending treatment to 28-32 sessions was associated with a 71% remission rate versus 34% for those terminated at session 20 (p<0.001). Premature termination (defined as ending therapy while PHQ-9 ≥10) was associated with a 2.4-fold increased risk of relapse within 12 months (95% CI: 1.8-3.2). CONCLUSIONS: For recurrent MDD, 20 sessions are often insufficient to achieve remission, particularly for patients still in the moderate severity range. Session limits that terminate treatment at 20 sessions for patients with PHQ-9 ≥10 may increase relapse risk and are not supported by the evidence base.
articles.relevance: Directly supports Scenario 3 — evidence that 20-session limit is insufficient for recurrent MDD patients with PHQ-9 ≥10, and premature termination increases relapse risk

articles.title: Relapse Rates Following Premature Psychotherapy Termination in Recurrent Major Depressive Disorder: A Prospective Cohort Study
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVE: To evaluate relapse rates when psychotherapy is terminated before achieving clinically meaningful response in patients with recurrent MDD. METHODS: Prospective cohort study of 1,236 adults with recurrent MDD (F33.x) receiving individual CBT. Patients were categorized by therapy termination status: (1) completed treatment (PHQ-9 <10 at termination, n=487), (2) premature termination due to insurance session limits (PHQ-9 ≥10 at termination, n=412), (3) patient-initiated dropout (n=337). Primary outcome was depressive episode recurrence within 18 months, assessed by structured clinical interview. RESULTS: At 18-month follow-up, relapse rates were: completed treatment 19%, premature insurance-terminated 54%, patient dropout 48% (p<0.001 between completed vs. insurance-terminated). Among insurance-terminated patients, those with PHQ-9 12-14 at termination had a relapse rate of 58% (95% CI: 51-65%), compared to 23% for patients with PHQ-9 5-9 at termination. Multivariate analysis identified insurance-mandated termination with PHQ-9 ≥10 as an independent predictor of relapse (HR 2.7, 95% CI: 2.1-3.5), after controlling for depression severity, episode count, and medication use. CONCLUSIONS: Insurance-driven premature termination of psychotherapy, particularly when patients remain in the moderate symptom range, is associated with significantly elevated relapse rates comparable to untreated dropout. These findings have implications for session limit policies and mental health parity compliance.
articles.relevance: Strongly supports Scenario 3 — premature termination at PHQ-9 12-14 has 58% relapse rate, directly applicable to patient with PHQ-9 = 12

articles.title: Mental Health Parity and Session Limits: Comparing Outpatient Treatment Limitations for Behavioral Health vs. Medical/Surgical Benefits in Commercial Insurance Plans
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: The Mental Health Parity and Addiction Equity Act (MHPAEA) prohibits health plans from imposing more restrictive treatment limitations on behavioral health benefits than on comparable medical/surgical benefits. However, enforcement of parity in quantitative treatment limits (session caps) remains inconsistent. METHODS: Cross-sectional analysis of 214 commercial insurance plans across 38 states, comparing outpatient treatment limitations for behavioral health (psychotherapy) versus medical/surgical (physical therapy, occupational therapy, speech therapy) services. RESULTS: 67% of plans imposed annual session limits on outpatient psychotherapy (median: 20 sessions/year). In contrast, only 31% imposed session limits on outpatient physical therapy (median: 30 sessions/year). Among plans with limits on both, the psychotherapy limit was lower than the physical therapy limit in 78% of cases (mean difference: 8.4 fewer sessions for psychotherapy). Only 12% of plans had documented parity analyses comparing their behavioral health and medical/surgical treatment limitations. Plans with 20-session psychotherapy limits that did not apply analogous limits to outpatient physical therapy were flagged as potentially non-compliant with MHPAEA quantitative treatment limit requirements. CONCLUSIONS: Significant disparities persist between behavioral health and medical/surgical outpatient treatment limitations in commercial insurance plans. Plans applying stricter session limits to psychotherapy than to comparable medical/surgical outpatient services may be in violation of MHPAEA.
articles.relevance: Supports Scenario 3 MHPAEA argument — evidence that 20-session psychotherapy limits may violate parity when comparable medical/surgical services have higher limits

articles.title: Consolidation Phase CBT for Recurrent Depression: Preventing Relapse Through Extended Treatment
articles.abstract: IMPORTANCE: Major depressive disorder with a recurrent course (F33.x) has high relapse rates following acute-phase treatment. Consolidation (continuation) phase CBT may reduce relapse risk. OBJECTIVE: To determine whether continuation CBT (C-CBT) following acute-phase response reduces relapse rates compared to treatment termination in recurrent MDD. DESIGN, SETTING, PARTICIPANTS: Randomized controlled trial at 8 academic medical centers. 524 adults with recurrent MDD who had responded to 16-20 sessions of acute-phase CBT (PHQ-9 decreased by ≥30% but remaining ≥10) were randomized to: (1) C-CBT (8-12 additional biweekly sessions) or (2) treatment termination with monitoring only. RESULTS: Over 24 months, relapse occurred in 26% of C-CBT participants versus 52% of termination participants (HR 0.42, 95% CI: 0.31-0.57, p<0.001). Number needed to treat (NNT) to prevent one relapse: 3.8. C-CBT was particularly effective for patients with 3+ prior episodes (relapse: 22% vs 61%, p<0.001) and those with PHQ-9 10-14 at randomization (relapse: 28% vs 59%, p<0.001). The mean total treatment course for C-CBT responders was 26 sessions (range: 22-32). CONCLUSIONS: Consolidation-phase CBT significantly reduces relapse in patients with recurrent MDD who have responded but not remitted after acute-phase treatment. Terminating therapy at 20 sessions while patients remain symptomatic (PHQ-9 ≥10) substantially increases relapse risk. An evidence-based course of CBT for recurrent MDD typically requires 24-32 total sessions.
articles.relevance: Strongly supports Scenario 3 — C-CBT after acute phase reduces relapse from 52% to 26%, NNT=3.8. Directly applicable to patient with PHQ-9=12 after 20 sessions.

articles.title: American Diabetes Association Standards of Care 2024: Glucose Monitoring Technology Recommendations
authors: American Diabetes Association Professional Practice Committee
articles.abstract: This section of the ADA Standards of Care addresses the use of glucose monitoring technologies in diabetes management. The ADA recommends that continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) be offered to all adults with type 2 diabetes who are on intensive insulin regimens, have a history of hypoglycemia, or have not achieved glycemic targets on current therapy. For patients with T2DM who have failed oral hypoglycemic therapy (metformin and/or sulfonylurea), CGM provides critical data for treatment decision-making, including identification of glycemic patterns, detection of asymptomatic hypoglycemia, and assessment of time-in-range metrics. The ADA position is that step therapy protocols requiring failure of multiple oral agents before CGM authorization are clinically appropriate but must not create barriers that delay access when step therapy failure is already documented. Insurance coverage policies should recognize documented step therapy completion as sufficient grounds for CGM authorization.
articles.relevance: Clinical guideline supporting Scenario 1 — ADA recommends CGM for T2DM patients who have failed oral therapy, and states documented step therapy completion should be sufficient for authorization

articles.title: American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons Clinical Practice Guideline: Management of Knee Pain and Suspected Meniscal Injury
articles.journal: Journal of the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons
articles.abstract: This clinical practice guideline provides evidence-based recommendations for the management of knee pain with suspected meniscal injury. Strong recommendation: MRI should be obtained when clinical examination reveals positive provocative tests (McMurray test, Apley grind test) with at least one of: joint effusion, mechanical symptoms (locking, catching), or failure to improve with 4-6 weeks of conservative therapy. Moderate recommendation: a trial of conservative physical therapy (4-6 weeks) is appropriate before MRI in patients with knee pain without clear mechanical symptoms or clinical examination findings suggestive of structural pathology. Limited recommendation: rigid time-based requirements for physical therapy duration (e.g., mandatory 6-week or 8-week minimums) before imaging authorization are not supported by the evidence and may delay diagnosis, particularly when clinical examination findings strongly suggest internal derangement. The guidelines emphasize that clinical judgment should guide imaging decisions, with physical therapy duration requirements serving as guidelines rather than absolute prerequisites.
articles.relevance: Supports Scenario 2 — AAOS guideline states rigid 6-week PT minimums are not evidence-based and may delay diagnosis when clinical signs (positive McMurray, effusion) suggest structural pathology

articles.title: APA Practice Guidelines for Major Depressive Disorder: Recommended Treatment Duration and Continuation Therapy
authors: American Psychiatric Association Guideline Development Panel
articles.abstract: The APA Practice Guidelines for MDD recommend that patients with recurrent major depressive disorder (3+ episodes) receive continuation-phase treatment for a minimum of 6-9 months following acute-phase response. For psychotherapy, this typically translates to 24-36 total sessions over 9-12 months for patients with recurrent MDD. The guidelines specifically address insurance session limits: 'Arbitrary annual session caps (e.g., 20 sessions/year) that do not account for diagnosis severity, recurrence history, or treatment response may result in premature treatment termination and increased relapse risk.' The APA recommends that treatment duration decisions be guided by clinical factors including: (1) number of prior episodes (patients with 3+ episodes require longer treatment), (2) current symptom severity (treatment should continue until sustained remission, typically PHQ-9 <5), (3) functional recovery (return to baseline occupational and social functioning), and (4) relapse risk factors (family history, early onset, comorbid anxiety). The guidelines emphasize the importance of shared decision-making between clinician and patient regarding treatment duration.
articles.relevance: Supports Scenario 3 — APA guidelines recommend 24-36 sessions for recurrent MDD and explicitly state that 20-session caps may cause premature termination
